Port 6421 phải nằm trong private network; port 6420 thường đi qua load balancer.

## rivet-dev/rivet (https://github.com/rivet-dev/rivet)
Description: The orchestrator for agentic workloads. A fast, high-density and scalable orchestrator for every workload an agent needs.
Homepage: https://www.rivet.dev
Language: Rust; license: Apache-2.0; created 2023-06-16; last push 2026-11-08
Latest release: v3.0.6 (2026-11-06)
README (start):
Fast, high-density, scalable orchestration with Rivet Actors.Built on S3 at SSD speeds.
  
    4.99 ms p99 cold starts, 72 KB RAM per Actor, scales to billions
  
  
    Quickstart •
    Documentation •
    Blog •
    Discord •
    X
  

## What is Rivet?

Rivet Actors are long-lived processes with in-memory state, a SQLite database, WebSockets, and scheduling. You can create one for each agent, user, session, or tenant.

- **72 KB per Actor**: Actors share a node process instead of each booting a sandbox, so one server holds hundreds of thousands.
- **4.99 ms p99 cold starts**: No image pull and no VM boot.
- **Built for scale**: All data lives in S3, so a cluster scales to billions of Actors.
- **Hibernates when idle, wakes on demand**: Idle Actors cost nothing and wake on the next request with nothing lost.
- **SQLite backed by S3, at SSD speeds**: 1.07 ms durable writes and 1.36 ms reads at p99, for about 10.4× less than replicated SSD storage.

### Use cases

- **[Durable & multiplayer AI agents](https://www.rivet.dev/guides/ai-agent)**: memory that survives restarts, shared live with every client
- **[Workflows](https://www.rivet.dev/workflows/docs)**: multi-step operations that replay instead of starting over
- **[AI-generated apps](https://www.rivet.dev/dynamic-apps/docs)**: run the apps and Actors your agent generates
- **[Collaborative editing](https://www.rivet.dev/guides/collaborative-text-editor)**: one Actor per document, synced to every editor

### Example

A minimal agent written from scratch. For a ready-made agent, use [Pi Durable](https://www.rivet.dev/agents/docs/quickstart/).

```typescript
// server.ts
import { actor, setup } from "rivetkit";
import { db } from "rivetkit/db";
import { streamText } from "ai";
import { openai } from "@ai-sdk/openai";

// One Actor per agent, created on first use: agent.getOrCreate(["agent-123"])
export const agent = actor({
  // 1. SQLite: every agent has its own database, so history survives restarts
  db: db({
    onMigrate: async (db) => {
      await db.execute("CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS messages (role TEXT, content TEXT)");
    },
  }),

  // 2. In-memory state: plain variables that live with the Actor, with no database round trip
  createVars: () => ({ online: new Map() }),

  // 3. WebSockets: each client holds a live connection, and the Actor pushes to all of them
  onDisconnect: (c, conn) => {
    c.vars.online.delete(conn.id);
    c.broadcast("online", [...c.vars.online.values()]);
  },

  actions: {
    join: (c, user: string) => {
      c.vars.online.set(c.conn.id, user);
      c.broadcast("online", [...c.vars.online.values()]);
    },

    sendMessage: async (c, text: string) => {
      // Save the message
      await c.db.execute("INSERT INTO messages VALUES (?, ?)", "user", text);
      const messages = await c.db.execute("SELECT role, content FROM messages");

      // Stream tokens to every connected client
      const response = streamText({ model: openai("gpt-5"), messages });
      for await (const delta of response.textStream) {
        c.broadcast("token", delta);
      }

      // Save the response
      await c.db.execute("INSERT INTO messages VALUES (?, ?)", "assistant", await response.text);
    },
  },
});

export const registry = setup({ use: { agent } });
```

```typescript
// client.ts (frontend or backend)
import { createClient } from "rivetkit/client";
import type { registry } from "./server";

const client = createClient();

// Open a WebSocket connection to the agent
const agent = client.agent.getOrCreate(["agent-123"]).connect();

// Listen for realtime events
agent.on("online", users => console.log("online:", users));
agent.on("token", delta => process.stdout.write(delta));

// Call actions on the Actor
await agent.join("nathan");
await agent.sendMessage("how many r's in strawberry?");
```

### Why run agents on Rivet Actors?

Each Actor gives the agent a **long-lived process** for long agent turns, **in-memory state** for context, a **WebSocket server** for multiplayer, **durable SQLite storage** for session transcripts and agent artifacts, and **hibernation** when idle.

Most of an agent's time is spent **waiting on inference**. When the agent loop runs inside a sandbox, you pay for a whole VM that sits **mostly idle** with low CPU usage.

Rivet Actors run the agent loop outside of the sandbox instead, often called **"separating the head from the hands."** The agent's state, memory, and context live in the Actor, and it reaches the sandbox through tools only when it needs to run code. This uses a fraction of the memory and limits the **blast radius** and **trust boundary** of the code it runs. Read more about [running the harness outside of the sandbox](https://www.rivet.dev/blog/2026-07-27-run-your-harness-outside-the-sandbox/).

### Do I need a sandbox with a Rivet Actor?

Often not. An agent needs a sandbox only to run code it writes. Developers on Rivet use three patterns:

- **Agents with tools**: Many agents only need tool calls, MCP, and APIs, such as customer support or personal agents. No sandbox needed.
- **Agents with a lightweight sandbox**: [agentOS](https://www.rivet.dev/agentos/docs) provides Linux-compatible sandboxing for JS and Python using V8 and WebAssembly, with full POSIX filesystems, networking stacks, and process trees. It covers most workloads, like data analysis, file processing, evals, and code mode.
- **Agents with a full sandbox**: Keep your existing sandbox provider and expose its shell and filesystem to the agent as tools, such as a `bash` tool that runs commands in the sandbox. The Actor reattaches to it across sleeps and restarts. See the [sandbox coding agent example](./examples/sandbox-coding-agent).

## Getting Started

### Use with your coding agent

Paste this prompt into Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, or any coding agent:

```text
Run npx skills add rivet-dev/skills, then ask me what to build and run it locally.
```

### Start from scratch

Rivet ships libraries built on top of Actors for common use cases.

- **[Actors](https://www.rivet.dev/actors/docs)**: Long-lived processes with state, realtime, and scheduling built in.
- **[Agents](https://www.rivet.dev/agents/docs)**: Durable agents built on Actors, with memory that survives restarts.
- **[Workflows](https://www.rivet.dev/workflows/docs)**: Multi-step operations built on Actors that replay instead of starting over.
- **[agentOS](https://www.rivet.dev/agentos/docs)**: Run the code your agent writes, securely, with granular control over network access, filesystem access, and resource limits.
- **[Dynamic Apps](https://www.rivet.dev/dynamic-apps/docs)** (preview): A backend per user, deployed the moment it is generated.

## How Actors compare to sandboxes

| Metric | Rivet Actor | Sandbox |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Cold start (p99) | **4.99 ms** | 1.70 s |
| Memory per instance | **72.4 KB** | 512 MiB |
| Storage | **SQLite on S3** | Disk per sandbox |
| Storage cost | **10.4× cheaper** | Replicated SSDs |

Benchmark details & methodology

- **Rivet numbers** come from the published [Rivet Actors vs Cloudflare Durable Objects benchmark](https://github.com/rivet-dev/bench-rivet-actors-vs-durable-objects), run on Rivet 3.0.3. Its repository has the raw samples and the scripts to reproduce them.
- **Sandbox numbers** are for [E2B](https://e2b.dev): 512 MiB is its default memory allocation from [E2B's billing documentation](https://docs.e2b.dev/billing) as of November 4, 2026, and 1.70 s is the p99 cold start from [ComputeSDK's October 30, 2026 sandbox benchmark](https://www.computesdk.com/benchmarks/sandboxes/burst-tti).
- **Storage cost** compares S3 Standard with three Amazon EBS gp3 copies at AWS list prices.
- Sources, dates, and the full method are at [rivet.dev/docs/benchmarking](https://www.rivet.dev/docs/benchmarking/).

## Features

- **Fault tolerance**: If a node goes down, its Actors move elsewhere with their state intact.
- **HTTP & WebSocket networking**: Call an Actor over HTTP or hold a live WebSocket to it.
- **End-to-end type safety**: Typed clients for your backend and React hooks for your frontend.
- **Cron & scheduling**: Wake an Actor on a schedule or at a time it sets for itself.
- **Actor-to-Actor calls**: Actors call each other by key across the cluster.
- **Scoped JWTs**: Give each client a [JWT](https://www.rivet.dev/docs/jwt) scoped to the Actors it may reach.
- **OpenTelemetry**: Traces, metrics, and logs in OTel format.

## Deployment Options

| Option | Description | Get started |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Local & self-host** | Run Rivet locally while you build. In production, run the control plane on Docker, Kubernetes, or a VM. S3 is the only dependency. | [Self-hosting docs](https://www.rivet.dev/docs/deploy/self-host/control-plane/) |
| **Rivet Cloud** | Fully managed, dedicated clusters on AWS or GCP in any region. Run your nodes on Rivet Cloud or bring your own. | [Dashboard](https://dashboard.rivet.dev) |
| **BYOC** | The control plane runs inside your own VPC on AWS, GCP, or Azure, fully managed by Rivet. Your data never leaves your cloud. | [BYOC docs](https://www.rivet.dev/docs/deploy/byoc/) |

Every option runs the same control plane, from local dev to production. [Talk to an engineer →](https://www.rivet.dev/talk-to-an-engineer)

## Works with the tools you already use

Typed SDKs for your backend and React hooks for your frontend. Rivet runs on native Node.js and Bun with no custom runtime, so your existing packages, tooling, and tests work unchanged.

**Deploy nodes on**: [Docker Compose](https://www.rivet.dev/docs/deploy/self-host/nodes/docker-compose/) • [Kubernetes](https://www.rivet.dev/docs/deploy/self-host/nodes/kubernetes/) • [VM & bare metal](https://www.rivet.dev/docs/deploy/self-host/nodes/vm/) • [Hetzner](https://www.rivet.dev/docs/deploy/self-host/nodes/hetzner/) • [AWS ECS](https://www.rivet.dev/docs/deploy/self-host/nodes/aws-ecs/) • [Railway](https://www.rivet.dev/docs/deploy/self-host/nodes/railway/) • [Render](https://www.rivet.dev/docs/deploy/self-host/nodes/render/)

**Frameworks**: [React](https://www.rivet.dev/actors/docs/clients/react) • [Effect](./examples/ai-agent-effect)

**Runtimes**: [Node.js](https://www.rivet.dev/actors/docs/quickstart/backend) • [Bun](https://www.rivet.dev/actors/docs/quickstart/backend) • [Rust](https://www.rivet.dev/actors/docs/quickstart/rust)

**Tools**: [Vitest](https://www.rivet.dev/actors/docs/testing) • [OpenTelemetry](https://www.rivet.dev/docs/tracing) • [Pino](https://www.rivet.dev/actors/docs/logging) • [AI SDK](./examples/ai-agent) • [OpenAPI](./rivetkit-openapi) • [AsyncAPI](./rivetkit-asyncapi)

[Request an integration →](https://github.com/rivet-dev/rivet/issues/new)

## FAQ

Does Rivet have BYOC?

Yes. Rivet deploys into your own cloud account, including air-gapped environments: the control plane and storage run inside your VPC while Rivet operates them. See the [BYOC docs](https://www.rivet.dev/docs/deploy/byoc/).

Does Rivet have a cloud?

Yes. [Rivet Cloud](https://dashboard.rivet.dev) runs fully managed, dedicated clusters on AWS or GCP in any region. It can run your app's Docker image as [nodes on Rivet Cloud](https://www.rivet.dev/docs/deploy/cloud/compute/), or you can [bring your own nodes](https://www.rivet.dev/docs/deploy/self-host/nodes/).

Can I self-host Rivet?

Yes. Rivet is fully self-hostable; see the [self-hosting docs](https://www.rivet.dev/docs/deploy/self-host/control-plane/). The control plane runs anywhere a container runs, with guides for Docker Compose, Kubernetes, VMs and bare metal, Hetzner, Railway, Render, and AWS ECS. For enterprise support with a self-hosted deployment, [contact us](https://www.rivet.dev/enterprise/).

Do I still need Postgres, FoundationDB, or NATS?

No. An object storage bucket is the only dependency: there is no database to run and no message bus, and control plane instances find each other through the bucket. Rivet works with Amazon S3, Goog

## Inomy-shop/allen (https://github.com/Inomy-shop/allen)
Description: Allen is an open-source AI engineering team that runs on your repos — specialist agents, deterministic orchestration through workflows, and approval gates you control. Drive it from chat, Slack, or Linear.
Homepage: https://askallen.build/
Language: TypeScript; license: MIT; created 2026-04-19; last push 2026-09-04
Latest release: v0.1.25 (2026-07-25)
README (start):
# Allen

> An agentic operating system for software development — assign work to a coordinated org of AI agents, watch them execute against real repositories, intervene at checkpoints, and improve them over time.

**Website:** 

Allen runs a multi-team organization of AI agents against your codebases. You talk to it in chat or hand it a Linear ticket; team-lead agents plan and delegate to specialist coding agents; work runs in isolated git worktrees with live terminals; every step is traced, every output is an artifact, and humans approve at defined checkpoints. It integrates with GitHub, Linear, Slack, MCP servers, Claude Code, and Codex.

> **Status: early alpha.** Run it against dedicated workspaces and disposable or non-critical repositories first. Review workflow and agent definitions before pointing it at code you care about.

---

## Table of contents

- [What Allen does](#what-allen-does)
- [Core concepts](#core-concepts)
- [Quickstart](#quickstart)
- [First workflow](#first-workflow)
- [Feature tour](#feature-tour)
- [Architecture](#architecture)
- [Default ports](#default-ports)
- [Configuration](#configuration)
- [Integrations](#integrations)
- [Development](#development)
- [Documentation](#documentation)
- [Security](#security)
- [Contributing](#contributing)
- [License](#license)

---

## What Allen does

- **Chat-driven agent work.** Open a chat, describe a task, and Allen routes it to the right agent or workflow. Agents can delegate to other agents; the full delegation tree is visible. Export any chat as a portable JSON bundle (messages, executions, logs, traces, artifacts) with configurable redaction, and import the bundle on another Allen instance for read-only replay.
- **A seeded agent org.** On first boot Allen seeds 6 teams (executive, product, engineering, quality, meta, unassigned) and 20+ agents — team leads that orchestrate and specialists that write code, review, test, document, investigate bugs, and resolve PR feedback.
- **YAML workflows.** Multi-step pipelines with agent nodes, code nodes, conditionals, parallel branches, sub-workflows, and human checkpoints. Nine workflows ship built-in (planning, bug fix, feature implementation, PR review resolution, self-healing, and more).
- **Isolated workspaces.** Every coding task runs in a dedicated git worktree with a live terminal (WebSocket PTY), file watcher, and a reverse proxy to preview dev servers.
- **Full execution observability.** Traces, per-node logs, tool calls, costs and token usage breakdown (cached input, non-cached input, output), checkpoints, artifacts, and a Mermaid graph of every workflow.
- **Human-in-the-loop.** Workflows pause at intervention points (approval, question, escalation) and wait for a person.
- **Integrations.** GitHub (PR sync, CodeRabbit comment resolution), Linear (ticket dispatch to agents/workflows), Slack (chat from a thread), and MCP servers (Postgres, custom tools, etc.).
- **Self-healing.** An hourly monitor watches Allen's own runtime, fingerprints incidents, files Linear tickets, and can auto-dispatch a bug-fix workflow.
- **Learning/memory.** Agents capture and retrieve learnings (facts, patterns, mistakes) scoped to global/workflow/context/agent, backed by embeddings.

## Core concepts

| Concept | What it is |
|---|---|
| **Agent** | A configured LLM persona (system prompt, model, tools, MCP allowlist, delegation targets). Team agents orchestrate; specialist agents do the hands-on work. Deleted agents are soft-deleted (`isDeleted=true`) and hidden from all surfaces; recreating one with the same name restores the original record. |
| **Team** | A group of agents with a lead and a parent team. Defines the delegation org chart. Teams with active members cannot be deleted. Deleted teams are soft-deleted and hidden; recreating with the same name restores the record. |
| **Workflow** | A YAML pipeline of nodes (`agent`, `code`, `human`, `condition`, `workflow`) connected by edges, with parallel branches and retries. Deleted workflows are soft-deleted and hidden; recreating with the same name restores the original record. |
| **Execution** | One run of a workflow or a single spawned agent. Has state, traces, logs, tool calls, artifacts. |
| **Workspace** | An isolated git worktree for a repo where agents run, with a terminal and preview proxy. |
| **Chat session** | A conversation with an agent. Can spawn agents, run workflows, and delegate. |
| **Intervention** | A human checkpoint where a workflow pauses for approval/input. |
| **Artifact** | A versioned output such as a design note, validation report, or generated file, addressable by a capability URL. |
| **Learning** | A captured insight injected into future agent prompts by scope. |
| **MCP server** | A Model Context Protocol tool server exposed to agents; configured per-server with `ALLEN_`-prefixed env vars. |

## Quickstart

### Requirements

`./scripts/setup.sh` checks for and (where possible) installs everything below — including Node 22 itself via nvm if it is missing:

- Node.js 22+ and npm 10+
- Git
- MongoDB 7 (auto-installed on macOS via Homebrew; install instructions printed for other OSes)
- **Claude Code CLI — required.** Installed via the official standalone installer (`curl -fsSL https://claude.ai/install.sh | bash`); the engine drives it with its `--agent` flag. You need an Anthropic account to authenticate it.
- **Codex CLI — optional.** Installed via `npm install -g @openai/codex`. Allen's chat defaults to Codex; set `ALLEN_DEFAULT_CHAT_PROVIDER=claude-cli` in `.env` to use Claude Code for chat instead and skip the OpenAI account entirely.

Supported platforms: macOS and Linux (and WSL2 on Windows). Native Windows is not supported.

### 1. Clone

```bash
git clone https://github.com/Inomy-shop/allen.git
cd allen
```

### 2. Run setup

```bash
./scripts/setup.sh
```

The setup script, in order:

1. Verifies npm 10+ and git, and installs Node 22 via nvm if Node is missing or older than 22.
2. Checks/installs MongoDB 7 (macOS via Homebrew) and ensures it is reachable on `localhost:27017`.
3. Installs the standalone Claude Code CLI via the official installer if missing or if the one on `PATH` lacks `--agent` support.
4. Installs the Codex CLI via npm if missing.
5. Runs `npm install` across all workspace packages.
6. Creates `.env` from `.env.example`, generates `JWT_ACCESS_SECRET` / `JWT_REFRESH_SECRET`, and auto-pins `CLAUDE_BIN` to the verified standalone CLI.
7. Prompts whether to install the optional Cognee-backed context engine. Pressing Enter skips it; run `npm run setup:context` later to install it.
8. Runs `npm run health` and prints PASS/FAIL per dependency.

Re-running is safe — it skips work already done and preserves your `.env`. If a step fails the script exits with a red error line; see [docs/troubleshooting.md → Setup Script Fails](docs/troubleshooting.md#setup-script-fails) for the fix matrix.

### 3. Authenticate the CLIs (one-time)

```bash
claude    # log in with your Anthropic account
codex     # optional: log in with your OpenAI account (skip if using claude-cli for chat)
```

Both CLIs persist auth on disk after first login.

### 4. Build and start Allen

The packages compile to `dist/` and the engine is consumed as a built dependency, so build before starting:

```bash
npm run build
npm start
```

This starts the API server on `http://localhost:4023` and the UI on `http://localhost:5173`.

### 5. Create the first admin

Open `http://localhost:5173`. On a fresh instance Allen opens an onboarding flow: create the first admin account → health check → register a repository → run a first workflow. After any user exists, the first-admin bootstrap endpoint closes and you sign in normally.

You can re-run the dependency checks any time:

```bash
npm run health
```

## First workflow

Use a disposable or non-critical repository for the first run — agents inspect files, and implementation workflows can write code, create branches, and open PRs.

1. Register a repository (local path, or clone from a GitHub SSH URL) on the Agents → Repos screen.
2. Open **Workflows** and choose `bug-fix-by-severity`.
3. Select the repo and enter a bug report (e.g. "Clicking Delete on an empty workflow crashes the UI with 'Cannot read property id of undefined'").
4. Watch the execution: timeline, node logs, tool calls, artifacts, and the opened PR.
5. Once you trust the output, try `feature-plan-and-implement` for a new-feature run.

Built-in workflows in `packages/engine/workflows/`:

| Workflow | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `feature-plan-and-implement.yml` | Take a user-supplied feature request, produce a technical design, implement, validate, and open a PR. |
| `bug-fix-by-severity.yml` | Triage a bug by severity and dispatch the appropriate fix path. |
| `tdd-design-by-severity.yml` | Generate a technical design from a user-supplied request, scaled to severity. |
| `milestone-implementation-from-prd-tdd.yml` | Implement milestones from existing product and technical design artifacts. |
| `agent-build-with-review.yml` | Research, review, validate, and create new Allen agents through a human-approved blueprint workflow. |
| `resolve-pr-reviews.yml` | Resolve CodeRabbit/PR review comments, run tests, push fixes, summarize. |
| `self-healing-incident-triage.yml` | Classify and route a production/runtime incident. |
| `allen-self-healing-monitor-hourly.yml` | Hourly scan of Allen's own runtime; files and dispatches incidents. |
| `multi-repo-change-orchestration.yml` | Parent orchestrator for cross-repo change delivery — clarify, plan per-repo work, approve, then run child workflows. |

See [`docs/first-workflow.md`](docs/first-workflow.md) for a step-by-step walkthrough.

## Feature tour

**Chat & delegation.** Talk to any agent. `@mention` workflows, repos, agents, or Linear tickets (`@ENG-123`). Agents delegate to other agents; conversation threads are persisted and the delegation tree is visible in the execution view.

**Visual workflow builder.** Build workflows in the UI (`/workflows/new`) by wiring agent/condition/parallel/human nodes, or check YAML into `packages/engine/workflows/`. The engine validates structure on load and renders a Mermaid graph.

**Workspaces.** Each coding task gets a git worktree under `/worktrees/`. Clicking a workspace in the sidebar opens it in a **workspace-mode chat** (`/chat?workspaceId=…`): a browser-style tab strip of linked chats with `+ New Chat`, close/restore, and a context bar showing the repo, branch, and worktree path. Agents in a workspace-linked chat automatically run with `cwd` set to the worktree. The Workspaces page (accessible from the context bar) still gives you the live terminal, file browser, and dev-server preview proxy.

**Executions & traces.** The Executions page lists running and recent runs (paginated, filterable). Drill into any execution for the node timeline, per-node logs, tool calls with payloads, token usage breakdown (cached input, non-cached input, output — per-node and execution totals), cost accounting, checkpoints, and artifacts.

**Chat export/import.** Export any chat session as a downloadable JSON bundle that includes messages, tool calls, execution trees, logs, traces, artifacts, interventions, watcher state, and code-diff snapshots. Toggles control what goes in; redaction options sanitise paths, identity, and secrets. Import a bundle on another Allen instance: a preview step shows counts and warnings, then the import creates a new local chat clearly labelled as read-only replay with disabled composer and a persistent banner.

**Multi-window desktop.** The Electron desktop app supports multiple independent windows (File → New Window, Cmd+N, or macOS Dock right-click → New Window). Each window shares the same backend but navigates independently — working in one window on Chat while another browses Workspaces, for instance. Closing a window does not shut down the shared runtime or affect other open windows. See [Desktop module]

Self-Host
Control Plane

What you run to self-host Rivet: control plane instances, a bucket, a disk per instance, and your nodes.

Self-hosting Rivet means running four things on your own infrastructure:

Part	What it is	How many
Control plane instance	The rivetdev/engine image. Every instance is identical and runs every service.	1 to try Rivet, 3 or more in production
Disk	A persistent local disk for each instance. It holds recent writes and the instance’s identity.	One per instance, never shared
Bucket	An object storage bucket (S3, S3-compatible, Google Cloud Storage or Azure Blob Storage). It holds the durable copy of every Rivet Actor’s data.	One per cluster
Nodes	Your app, running the Rivet SDK. Nodes connect out to the control plane and host your Rivet Actors.	As many as you need

There is no database to run and no message bus. Control plane instances find each other through the bucket.

BACKEND
Clients
Browsers, apps
Actor nodes
Your code
Control plane
Schedule, route, persist
Object storage
S3, GCS or Azure

Nodes reach the control plane on port 6420, usually through a load balancer. Instances also talk to each other on port 6421, which stays on your private network. See Ports & TLS.

Each Rivet Actor’s data is replicated across the disks of several instances as soon as it is written, then moved to the bucket in the background. Losing one instance loses no data. See Storage.

The control plane runs in one region. Multi-region self-hosting is coming. See Multi-Region.

Picking a guide
If you want	Use
A single instance to try Rivet	Docker Compose
A production cluster	Kubernetes
Linux hosts you already own	VM & bare metal
Hetzner Cloud	Hetzner
A single instance on a managed platform	Railway or Render
AWS	AWS ECS
Anything else	Custom platform
Run your app against the control plane	Nodes

For the lowest latency, use the VM & bare metal or Hetzner guide on machines with local NVMe disks. Kubernetes pods do not get raw NVMe. See Benchmarking.

## Docker Compose | Rivet Node Self-Host - Rivet
URL: https://rivet.dev/docs/deploy/self-host/nodes/docker-compose/
Description: Run Rivet nodes with Docker Compose. Explore Docker Compose in Rivet Node Self-Host with practical guidance, configuration details, and production-ready…

Skip to main content
Toggle navigation menu
Sign In
Copy Markdown
Platforms
Docker Compose

Run Rivet nodes with Docker Compose.

Your container runs as a node: it opens a connection out to the control plane on startup. It needs no published port.

Requirements

A namespace and a node pool created with PUT /pools/{pool} (see Nodes & Node Pools). In local development, RivetKit creates the default pool for you.

Docker with the Compose plugin
A running control plane
Steps
Package your app
FROM node:24-slim
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci --omit=dev
COPY . .
CMD ["node", "server.js"]

CMD invokes the binary directly rather than npm start, so the process receives SIGTERM and can drain.

Rivet requires Node.js 22 or newer.

Add the service

stop_grace_period matters here. Each Rivet Actor gets up to 15 seconds to save its state, and Compose’s default of 10 seconds can cut them off.

services:
  my-app:
    build: .
    environment:
      RIVET_ENDPOINT: "${RIVET_ENDPOINT}"
    stop_grace_period: 60s
    restart: unless-stopped

The endpoint value is described in Deploy Nodes. Put it in a .env file next to the Compose file and keep it out of version control.

Run alongside a self-hosted control plane

When both halves live in the same Compose file, the node reaches the control plane by service name over the Compose network:

  my-app:
    build: .
    environment:
      RIVET_ENDPOINT: "http://default:${RIVET_TOKEN}@rivet:6420"
    depends_on:
      - rivet
    stop_grace_period: 60s
    restart: unless-stopped

See the control plane guide for the other half of this file.

Start it
docker compose up -d

Verify
docker compose ps

The service should be running. Call one of your Rivet Actors to confirm it responds.

Scaling

Compose has no autoscaler. Nodes are interchangeable, so docker compose up -d --scale my-app=3 adds replicas that all join the same pool, but they share one host’s CPU and memory. For capacity beyond a single host, or for autoscaling, move to Kubernetes or ECS.

Keep stop_grace_period: 60s on every replica. Scaling down cuts actors off otherwise.

Description: Create and run your first Rivet Actor with Node.js or Bun, define typed actions, and connect through the JavaScript client.

Skip to main content

Quickstart
Node.js & Bun Quickstart

Create and run your first Rivet Actor with Node.js or Bun, define typed actions, and connect through the JavaScript client.

Prefer to start from a complete project? See the runnable hello-world example.

Steps
Add Rivet Skill to Coding Agent (Optional)

If you’re using an AI coding assistant (like Claude Code, Cursor, Windsurf, etc.), add Rivet skills for enhanced development assistance:

npx skills add rivet-dev/skills

Install Rivet
npm install rivetkit

Create Actors and Start Server

Create a file with your actors, set up the registry, and start the server:

import { actor, setup } from "rivetkit";
import { db } from "rivetkit/db";

export const counter = actor({
	db: db({
		onMigrate: async (db) => {
			await db.execute(
				"CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS counter (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY CHECK (id = 1), count INTEGER NOT NULL)",
			);
			await db.execute("INSERT OR IGNORE INTO counter (id, count) VALUES (1, 0)");
		},
	}),
	actions: {
		increment: async (c, x: number) => {
			const [{ count }] = await c.db.execute<{ count: number }>(
				"UPDATE counter SET count = count + ? WHERE id = 1 RETURNING count",
				x,
			);
			c.broadcast("newCount", count);
			return count;
		},
	},
});

export const registry = setup({
	use: { counter },
});

registry.start();

Show more
Run Server
Node.js
Bun
Deno
npx tsx --watch index.ts

Your server is now running on http://localhost:6420. Clients connect directly to the Rivet control plane on this port.

Connect To The Rivet Actor

This code can run either in your frontend or within your backend:

TypeScript
React
client.ts
import { createClient } from "rivetkit/client";
import type { registry } from "./index";

const client = createClient<typeof registry>("http://localhost:6420");

// Get or create a counter actor for the key "my-counter"
const counter = client.counter.getOrCreate(["my-counter"]);

// Call actions
const count = await counter.increment(3);
console.log("New count:", count);

// Listen to realtime events
const connection = counter.connect();
connection.on("newCount", (newCount: number) => {
	console.log("Count changed:", newCount);
});

// Increment through connection
await connection.increment(1);

See the JavaScript client documentation for more information.

Deploy

In development, Rivet runs a local control plane for you and keeps Actor data on your machine.

To scale Rivet in production, pick how much of it you want to run yourself:

Fully managed
Rivet runs the control plane and your nodes. Nothing to operate.
Bring your own compute
Rivet runs the control plane. Your nodes run on your own infrastructure.
Full self-hosting
You run the control plane and your nodes. No dependency on Rivet Cloud.

If you are running your own nodes, follow the guide for your hosting provider:

Docker Compose
Kubernetes
Virtual Machine
Hetzner
AWS ECS
Railway
Render
Custom Platform
Configuration Options
Server Setup: Different ways to run your server with serve(), handler(), or framework adapters.
Clients: Connect to Actors from JavaScript, React, or other platforms.
Authentication: Secure Actor connections with custom authentication logic.
CORS: Configure origin restrictions to secure your Actors from unauthorized access.
Logging: Configure logging output for debugging and monitoring.
Nodes & Node Pools: Run your app as long-lived nodes grouped into node pools.

URL: https://rivet.dev/docs/jwt/
Description: Issue short-lived JWTs with explicit permissions in one namespace. Explore Scoped Tokens in Rivet documentation with practical guidance, configuration…

Skip to main content
Toggle navigation menu
Sign In
Copy Markdown
Authentication
Scoped Tokens

Issue short-lived JWTs with explicit permissions in one namespace.

A scoped token gives its holder selected permissions in one namespace. Issue it on your backend with the control plane’s admin credential, then return only the scoped token to the application.

Quickstart
Issue a token

This example grants read access to Actor traffic in the production namespace. Every holder can reach every Actor in that namespace; use a specific Actor ID for private per-user access.

curl -X POST "$RIVET_API/auth/tokens" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $RIVET_ADMIN_TOKEN" \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{
    "namespace": "production",
    "duration": 900,
    "grants": [
      {"resource":"actor_gateway","target":"any","operations":["read"]}
    ]
  }'

The response contains token, issued_ts, and expires_ts. Timestamps are Unix milliseconds; duration is seconds.

Use the token

Set $RIVET_TOKEN to the returned token and call an Actor’s gateway endpoint:

curl "$RIVET_API/gateway/$ACTOR_ID/health" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $RIVET_TOKEN"

This grant does not allow Actor creation, listing, node registration, or pool management.

Grants

Each grant names a resource, a target, and operations drawn from create, read, update, delete, and list. A target is "any" or an object such as {"id":"<actor-id>"}. Replace the placeholder with the resolved Actor ID.

Resource	Purpose
actor	Create, resolve, list, or manage Actors.
actor_gateway	Reach an Actor’s actions, events, or HTTP handlers.
node	Register or inspect nodes.
pool	Read or manage node pool configuration.

Actor management and gateway access require separate grants. Permission to reach one Actor does not allow the holder to create other Actors. Namespace administration and token issuance require the admin credential.

Inspect and renew
curl "$RIVET_API/auth/tokens/inspect" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $RIVET_TOKEN"

The response contains the namespace slug, grants, subject, and issue and expiry timestamps. Renew expiring credentials through your authenticated backend. Do not give clients the admin credential to renew tokens themselves.
